summary:
Lunar Exploration Guide is a website that makes lunar landing site evaluation fast and intuitive. Users choose from Apollo sites, CLPS targets, and international missions, or enter custom coordinates, then pick a date and time and add scenarios for side-by-side comparison. The app computes Sun and Earth positions from JPL ephemeris data, including libration, and draws them against a horizon built from LOLA topography. A horizon view, sunset and Earthset timelines, and a lunar-day timeline show sunlight duration, solar elevation (a proxy for power), and direct-to-Earth communication windows, with a viable/marginal/not-viable summary for each scenario.
This addresses the challenge’s core gap: tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons are built for specialists, making scenario comparison slow. Our tool turns raw ephemeris and terrain data into clear visuals, so teams can quickly compare sites and dates.
It matters because launch delays and hardware setbacks often force teams to change their landing date or site, and at the south pole, a few kilometers or days can decide whether a mission has power and communications. Toggles that hide technical data also let students and the public see why lunar missions are so hard to plan.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Lunar Site Planner lets anyone pick a spot on the Moon and see when it gets sunlight and when it can talk to Earth, for any date. It runs in a web browser and is built entirely from NASA data.

  • 3D Moon: a sunlit globe built from NASA laser altimeter terrain and photo mosaics, with the Sun and Earth placed in their true directions. Click anywhere to choose a site.
  • View from the site: a ground-level view of what you would see standing there, with the real skyline, the Sun, and Earth showing its current phase.
  • Sunlight meter: how much solar power a site gets, on flat ground and on a panel facing the Sun, including when the Sun is partly hidden behind terrain.
  • Data panel: sunlight and communication windows, upcoming sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset, and side-by-side comparison of sites or date ranges, with export for further work.
  • Site library: historic and planned landing sites, polar sites and science targets, plus any points users drop themselves.
  • Time controls: choose a start date and span, then play or step through time.

Visibility accounts for terrain. For each site the app traces the surrounding skyline from real elevation data, including the Moon's curvature, and only counts the Sun or Earth as visible when it is above that skyline.

Behind the planner is a lunar orbit simulator that models the Moon's uneven gravity and the pull of the Sun and Earth, and stops a trajectory when it hits the terrain.

Benefits

  • It answers the two questions that decide a landing site: will a lander get power, and can it talk to Earth? Both come as dated windows, not rough averages.
  • It is terrain-aware. Crater rims and mountains block the Sun and Earth, which matters most at the poles, and flat-ground models miss this.
  • It is free and easy to reach. It runs as a website with no install, account or server, and a Python version runs locally.
  • It is checked. We tested the model against independent NASA data before trusting it.
  • It makes comparison quick. Saved sites or date ranges sit side by side, and results can be exported.

Intended impact

We want lunar site planning to be something students, educators and small mission teams can do in a browser, not only space agencies.

  • Mission planning: with Artemis and commercial landers heading to the south pole, teams need fast first looks at power and communication for candidate sites.
  • Education: students can see why a polar crater rim gets near-constant sunlight while a crater floor stays dark, and why Earth never rises over the far side.
  • Open NASA data in use: the project shows how several separate NASA datasets can be combined into one tool that non-experts can use.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS and MATLAB.
  • Python libraries: NumPy and SciPy for the maths and orbit integration, Numba to speed up the gravity calculations, and Plotly, Matplotlib, Pillow and tifffile for graphics and image data.
  • Web front end: Plotly.js for the 3D Moon and charts, and HTML canvas for the site view and mini map.
  • Hosting: a static website generated by a Python build script and deployed through GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages.
  • NASA data: LRO LOLA terrain, NASA Moon Trek imagery and feature names, LROC QuickMap, the JPL Horizons API for Sun and Earth positions, GRAIL gravity data, and NASA NAIF data for the Moon's orientation.
  • Development: Git and GitHub, and Claude Code.

How it is creative

  • You stand on the Moon. Most lunar tools show a map from above; ours also shows the sky from the ground, with the real skyline and a changing Earth.
  • Many NASA sources in one place. Terrain, imagery, feature names, gravity and planetary positions usually live in separate tools. We combined them into one consistent model.
  • Real sunlight, not just day and night. The sunlight meter connects what you see to what a solar panel would actually produce.
  • It works with no server. Browsers can't query NASA's position service directly, so we pre-compute Sun and Earth positions ahead of time and package them with the site, keeping it small and fast.
  • A flexible workspace. Panels can be dragged, resized and minimised, so users can arrange the screen the way a mission planner would.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: we checked each part of the model against independent NASA data, including the Moon's orientation, our gravity map, two separate terrain datasets, and orbit predictions against a real spacecraft. These checks caught and fixed real bugs, including a sign error in a frame rotation and a pixel alignment issue in one data source.
  • Terrain: at the poles the Sun stays near the horizon, so ignoring terrain would give wrong answers exactly where missions are going.
  • Speed and size: we download only the level of gravity detail needed and compile the heavy maths, and the website pre-computes positions so it loads quickly.
  • Ease of use: we sketched a wireframe first, then built a layout with named mission sites, clear buttons and keyboard shortcuts.
  • Access: a free website for anyone, plus Python and MATLAB versions for people who want to run it themselves.
  • Honest limits: spacecraft maneuvers are not modelled, solar radiation pressure uses a simple model and is off by default, and some image-based terrain tiles were too coarse for calculations, so we used higher-quality elevation data instead.
